EntertainmentTab.title: New Inbetweeners film confirmed by Netflix as lead stars return
EntertainmentTab.text:
Ooh, sequel friend! A new Inbetweeners movie is officially in the works, Netflix has confirmed.

The original cast of Simon Bird, James Buckley, Blake Harrison and Joe Thomas will reprise their roles for the feature film, with production starting on Monday.

The Inbetweeners 3 will follow on the story of their characters, Will McKenzie, Jay Cartwright, Neil Sutherland and Simon Cooper.

They originally starred in three seasons of the popular coming-of-age sitcom, which aired on E4 between 2008 and 2010.

It followed their trials and misadventures as suburban teenagers at the fictional Rudge Park Comprehensive as they navigated school life and friendship.

The show has gained new fans over the years due to some of its best bits finding new life on social media, as well as through the film sequels.

The third instalment follows two sequels backed by Film4, which were released in 2011 and 2014.

Alongside the announcement, Netflix released a teaser video which showed Will, Simon, Neil and Jay return to their iconic yellow Fiat.

The friend group all get into the tiny car but Simon struggles to start the engine.

After some encouragement, it gets going and they drive out of what looks like a storage unit.

EntertainmentTab.title: Dizzee Rascal spotted at Wallingford community folk festival
EntertainmentTab.text:
Music lovers were surprised by the "unexpected" arrival of rapper Dizzee Rascal during a market town's folk festival.

They had been attending the BunkFest weekend in Wallingford, Oxfordshire, on Sunday, when the superstar was seen at The Boat House pub.

Several people rushed over to have their photos taken with the grime and hip hop artist, who has so far had five UK number one singles, including Bonkers, Dance Wiv Me and Holiday.

Festival attendee Charlie Garwood, 23, said: "I love his songs. You don't expect someone like that to be in a little town like Wallingford."

The lab technician from Benson said Dizzee told him he was "just seeing a friend" when he bumped into him in the street.

He believes he then got on a private boat on the River Thames.

Garwood told his parents, who initially did not believe him and assumed the photo was AI.

"It's so unexpected," he told the BBC.

"It's one of those things you just don't believe at first. He's known for his dance anthems, we grew up listening to him... it's just a cool thing."

EntertainmentTab.title: Musk review – epic study of the world’s richest and most banal man
EntertainmentTab.text:
‘Elon is a nuke.” The speaker is Ashley St Clair, a former conservative Maga influencer and one of Elon Musk’s former girlfriends-slash-baby mommas.

She is a fascinating expert witness in Alex Gibney’s four-hour epic study of the world’s richest and dullest man: the overgrown brattish South-African-born trillionaire plutocrat, ersatz visionary and Trump courtier who owns Tesla cars, SpaceX rocket ships, Starlink satellites on which nation states’ military capabilities are increasingly reliant, X (formerly Twitter) which shapes the collective “incel” id of billions and GrokAI whose vast server farms daily guzzle oceans of precious water.

As head of Trump’s incompetent cost-cutting Doge (Department of Government Efficiency) unit, Musk actually increased the US deficit by sacking thousands of revenue officers whose job was to rake in tax – while reportedly accessing and improperly sharing Americans’ sensitive social security data.

He does indeed look like a nuke, efficiently designed, destructive, seemingly unguided and uncontrolled.

Gibney’s excellent film covers a lot of ground in its extraordinary story, although we don’t get to hear about the mysterious process that changed a balding youngster into a follicularly unchallenged mature man.

Musk is a uniquely disquieting baseball-capped figure, grinning and giggling and smirking on a thousand sycophantic podcasts like a modern, hyper-evolved version of Anthony Trollope’s wealthy charlatan Augustus Melmotte in The Way We Live Now. But given Musk’s boyish love of space travel and sci-fi, Gibney wittily compares him to the hero of the 1936 film version of HG Wells’s The Man Who Could Work Miracles about godlike space aliens who capriciously confer supernatural powers on a banal, ordinary earthling.

Gibney doesn’t get to talk to Musk (or Trump) though in the spirit of Musk’s AI interests, he creates a photorealistic CG avatar who mouths all the things the man himself is reported as saying (a rather contrived visual joke, actually, which the film didn’t need). He speaks to many professional colleagues, and to Musk’s formidably opinionated father Errol Musk who fills us in on Elon’s formative years in the tense world of South Africa in which young Musk was bullied and beaten up.

Gibney speaks to Musk’s first wife Justine Musk (née Wilson), a passionate and intelligent woman who tells us about the tragedy of one of their infant children dying of Sids and then the hurt she felt when Elon felt the need to grandstand about this on social media, claiming the child had died in his arms (it was her arms, she says). And given that heart-wrenching death, how crass it was for him to announce later on social media that his trans daughter had “died” of “woke mind virus”. Much later, Musk showed a creepy enthusiasm for procreating many children with various women; Musk reportedly built compounds for his extended families like something from The Handmaid’s Tale.

Back in the 90s as a pushy, bright young tech innovator, Musk had started out by inventing and selling an online Yellow Pages-type site, got involved in Peter Thiel’s PayPal and cleaned up again when this was sold to eBay. He got involved in the electric automobile industry, giving us Teslas, while misleading the public about their range.

His SpaceX adventure and his preposterous and ignorant effusions about colonising Mars were spectacular advertisements for his personal brand – so important for inflating stock market valuation – especially when he did indeed invent rockets that could be landed and re-used. But the question of how and when these rockets will carry us to inhabitable planets remains unanswered. Both his cars and his rocket ships got him on the receiving end of millions of dollars of federal money and lines of credit.

And at the beginning of the 21st century he was still the darling of the liberal world and the Obama administration for an apparently compelling eco-vision for non-fossil-fuel cars.

All this changed when Joe Biden seemed to be casting a cold eye on Musk’s businesses, and Musk went all in on promoting Trump 2.0. In 2024 and was rewarded with that grotesque Doge sinecure, damaging American public finances – from which he had benefited so lavishly.

What is so absorbing about Gibney’s documentary is that it has the structure and rhetoric of a film that could be about, say, Elizabeth Holmes, disgraced inventor of the phoney blood-test, or Sam Bankman-Fried, the cryptocurrency fraudster, or Billy McFarland, promoter of the Fyre festival. All of these were media darlings in their day, supposed visionaries and feted disrupters, talking the talk in front of saucer-eyed believers.

Unlike these illusionists Musk does have actual palpable success, with Tesla being a long-standing profitable company and Space X, among other things inventing successful re-usable rockets, allied with a skill they don’t have in moving on from commodity to commodity, while controlling the means of production in social media and cultivating the presidency. Just as well because, if Musk were ever to fall, it would truly send shock waves through Wall Street, Washington and Silicon Valley.

EntertainmentTab.title: A constipated baby and a kid that looks like Boris Johnson: why would anyone bother stealing a Renoir?
EntertainmentTab.text:
Stealing from the Louvre you can understand. I mean, who wouldn’t want a Géricault or Leonardo to hang in the downstairs loo? Same for the Musée d’Orsay too, even the Pompidou – they’re French museums absolutely rammed full of stunning art, all just begging to be audaciously heisted. But the Renoir Museum? It’s hard to see why anyone would bother.

As French art fans reel at the news that two Renoir paintings were stolen from the Cagnes-sur-Mer museum that bears his name this week, the rest of the art world has been saying really? Him? Renoir? He’s … awful. It’s like doing a heist of flares in the era of skinny jeans.

Did the thieves know something the rest of us don’t? Or was this just a crime of opportunity, taking advantage of a regional art museum with shonky security?

Pierre-Auguste Renoir was one of impressionism’s head honchos, a leading figure in one of 19th-century art’s most important movements. But time hasn’t been too kind to poor old Pierre. Where his contemporaries like Monet, Cézanne and Degas have been heralded as modernist revolutionaries, artists who shaped the future of western painting and helped set the path that all of their successors would soon follow, in recent years Renoir has been denigrated, mocked, protested and hashtagged.

In 2015, a group who called themselves Renoir Sucks at Painting picketed the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, and then protested outside the Met in New York, with placards that read “God Hates Renoir” and “ReNOir”, demanding the museums remove his work from display. And they had their sympathisers: the hashtag #RenoirSucksatPainting trended soon after, they sold hundreds of anti-Renoir T-shirts, and their Instagram was full of photos of people giving the finger to Renoir paintings or pretending to vomit in front of them.

And his crime? Kitsch and chintziness. His work is soft focus and gentle, his figures are plump and joyful, it’s all happy haze and night-time revelry. He lacks the hard-edged absolute dedication to angular, prismatic experimentation that made the impressionists so famous. He is the safest of the group, the chocolate boxiest, the easiest, the horniest. And that has made him the most hated.

It’s not a new thing. Even his contemporaries disliked him. Édouard Manet said he had “no talent” and Mary Cassatt described his paintings of women as “the most awful of all”. Add to all of that a hefty dose of antisemitism (he refused to take part in exhibitions that featured Jewish impressionist Camille Pissarro), a big pinch of misogyny, and you’ve got a recipe of aesthetic distaste that can last centuries.

However in PR terms, the timing of this latest in a long string of French art robberies couldn’t be better. The National Gallery is opening their major Renoir and Love exhibition next month, a show they hope will have the same blockbuster success it had at the Musée d’Orsay in Paris this summer.

I want to defend Renoir, if only for the sake of debate, but I’ve hated his work for decades. I like him when he’s weird, when his nudes look like a super-psychedelic, ultra-horny version of Rubens with endless, surreal, undulating rolls of pink flesh. And I like a lot of his hazy, strange landscapes, though not as much as the work of any other impressionist. But for the most part, the haters are right.

I mean look at the works the thieves made off with after cutting through the fence with bolt cutters in the early hours of the morning. The first is Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano, her tiny head dwarfed by shoulders so vastly broad she could play rugby for Saracens, all watched over by a tiny painting-within-a-painting of a constipated looking baby. The other, Jeune Femme au Puits, is an unfinished smudge of a woman pulling a bucket out of a well. An art detective said the thieves would “have no idea what to do” with the paintings, well, they probably have some idea, and it involves the dustbin.

The best bit about this week’s heist on the Côte d’Azur is that the thieves actually took four paintings, but decided to leave two behind as they ran for it, including a portrait of a little boy who looks almost exactly like Boris Johnson. In all my years as an art critic, I’ve never managed a piece of criticism as incisive, cutting and direct as a bunch of criminals looking at a painting that they’d already nicked and thinking “leave it – it’s not worth it”.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘We all have an expiry date’: Kimberly Akimbo, the achingly funny musical about a teen with a 64-year-old body
EntertainmentTab.text:
Jeanine Tesori is thinking about her mother back home in the US. “She’s 95,” says the composer, “and she’s not been well. But she would look in the mirror and be like, ‘I can’t believe I’m old.’ It’s always a surprise, always. There’s an interiority about ageing, especially as women. You stay playful and you stay curious, but the world has other ideas.”

Ageing – and growing up, which is not necessarily the same thing – are a central consideration in the musical that Tesori has been rehearsing. Kimberly Akimbo, which the composer developed with David Lindsay-Abaire from his play, follows a teenage girl with a rare genetic condition that causes her to age at four times the normal rate. Its London debut stars the 66-year-old Maria Friedman as Kimberly. “And she has such a bright young energy,” says Tesori as we chat in a rough-and-ready rehearsal room in London, “that she doesn’t have to do anything to play 16.”

If a story about a girl with a life-shortening condition sounds like a tragedy, don’t be fooled. Kimberly Akimbo is a comedy about a chaotic family (from a hypochondriac mother to a criminal aunt) and a tender teenage romance. Uplifting and achingly funny, the original New York production was the biggest winner of the 2023 Tony awards. Tesori watched the London cast rehearse its bittersweet ending with her lips zipped firmly shut: “David and I know the show so well that we have to just let people interpret it their own way.”

For Tesori, a protagonist who knows she may not reach adulthood raises the question of how we use our time. “We all have an expiry date,” she says, recalling the line from Mary Oliver’s poem, The Summer Day: what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life? “I lost so many friends during the Aids crisis. I’m from that generation of watching these incredible people, mostly men, disappear. You become aware of how you live.”

At 64, her own life looks a fulfilled one: mother, teacher, legend of her industry. Her compositional dexterity and range, combined with an extraordinary ability to turn playwrights into lyricists and librettists, has produced everything from fun-packed Broadway shows (Thoroughly Modern Millie, Shrek), to complex, thought-provoking musicals (Soft Power, Caroline, or Change) and avant garde operas about police racism, drone pilots, and Eugene O’Neill’s marital rows.

“Everybody knows she’s a brilliant composer,” says Lindsay-Abaire, when he swings by rehearsals during lunch. “But she’s also one of the most insightful dramatists – she understands story structure and character and things that not all composers do or are even interested in.”

What Tesori’s projects have in common is her laser-sharp focus on emotional truth, be it in the powerfully orchestral blues and spirituals of Caroline, or Change – or the intimately interwoven harmonies and counterpoint of the three-handed chamber piece, Fun Home. The first UK production of that last one – an adaptation of Alison Bechdel’s celebrated autobiographical graphic novel – ran at Manchester’s Royal Exchange Theatre this summer and its director, Sarah Frankcom, calls it “a masterpiece”, adding: “Jeanine is able to express moments of profound change in people, in what is a very spare musical. The motifs coalesce and consolidate and lead you towards a last 15 minutes that are absolutely shattering.”

Tesori admits she’s drawn to dad-daughter stories, which are at the heart of Fun Home, Caroline, or Change and Kimberly Akimbo. Her own father died more than 20 years ago, but “the story lives on, and I think it helps me process – you try to answer the unanswerable question. My father was a very complicated man: a man of science who really wanted to be a fisherman. He wanted a simple life and he got anything but; he wanted sons and he got daughters.”

Tesori’s upbringing in a chaotic, multi-generational Italian family helped inspire some of Kimberly Akimbo’s scenes. (Her three sisters sound a hoot: not long ago one of them stole a picnic table from a park in broad daylight to prove that older women are invisible). It also played its part in her musical development. Tesori’s grandfather was a band arranger and violist who emigrated from Sicily – she still has his baton – and one of her sisters played piano while another had a vast record collection. “We listened to everybody from Stevie Wonder and Aretha Franklin to the Stones and the Beatles, Led Zeppelin, Carole King. Cat Stevens was huge in our house.”

That breadth of repertoire – encouraged by her first piano teacher – led Tesori outside the confines of classical academe, and fostered a musical versatility that has become the hallmark of her career. A recent trip to Jesus Christ Superstar blew her away, although she says it can be hard to relax and enjoy musical performances because her brain insists on analysing the scores. Instead, she has spent these weeks dipping into plays and comedy in off-West End and fringe venues: “That’s my favourite kind of theatre, to go in not knowing anything and just discover it.”

What about Broadway, which Andrew Lloyd Webber recently pronounced to be “in dire danger”? Tesori says she finds the capitalisation of its business models “scary” and feels a responsibility to find solutions for its increasing costs. “My job is to make things work better than when I leave – that’s the job of everybody who has been rewarded by the industry. When I started doing shows they were tearing Broadway houses down, because there were not enough shows to fill them. So I’ve always heard this chorus of ‘Broadway’s in trouble’, but for different reasons.”

She is a dedicated mentor (“I take that job seriously”) at a time when performing arts space in the US is being threatened and politicised. “It’s really frustrating,” she says, “and it’s very easy to feel hopeless. But I don’t. You could throw up your hands – but our job is to write.” She typically has three to four projects on the go, and has recently been researching a story in Naples, but never writes music for anything she doesn’t believe in. “Any show I do is going to be five years of concentrated work. That’s like graduate school plus a year. If I don’t understand it, I can’t say yes to it.”

She adds: “I love working with playwrights who are looking at the global conversation.” And her deep friendship with Lindsay-Abaire is obvious. “We both have a similar sense of humour,” he says. “We like dark, inappropriate comedy, which is why this show is funny and sad at the same time.”

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘Cantona’s a Kwengletarian!’ Inside the maximalist, magical mentality of rising London Irish rapper Kibo
EntertainmentTab.text:
A few Guinnesses into an interview in his local Irish boozer, and 26-year-old Harrow rapper Kibo is cooking. We’re talking football. As a kid, he preferred playing Fifa Street – where ordinary players backflip off walls to score incomprehensible bicycle kicks – to regular realistic Fifa. “If I’m gonna play a video game, I want to do some shit I can’t do in real life,” he says. He’s drawn to similarly miraculous footballers: Balotelli, Drogba in his Chelsea days, Ronaldinho and his dad’s favourite, Eric Cantona: “Oh God, with his collar popped, looking like Kanye West?” Kibo then recites Cantona’s 2019 Uefa president’s award speech – a mash-up of King Lear and philosophical musings on war and science – to near perfection.

Magic is at the heart of Kwelengletarianism, “the idea of being in a place that’s very grey, and trying to find a prismatic iridescence in it”, that underpins Kibo’s sensational album Kwengletaria: Ragamyff. (Cantona? “He’s a Kwengletarian to the nth degree.”) During his long rise through London’s rap scene, canonised by co-signs from Skepta, JME and Dave, Kibo has become a rare MC from Harrow, the town that produced Kate Nash and Jai Paul but no rappers of note. “It’s awesome,” he says of its lack of rap tradition, “a complete blank slate” to be as imaginative as he wants. Kwengletaria finds the myth in the mundane: on the track Bakerloo Dragon, a normal tube journey becomes a cruising broken-beat roller aboard a fire-spitting Bakerloo line train. I tell him my train to Harrow was one of these flame-graffitied dragons. “But did you get any sparks?” he asks enthusiastically. “You get sparks after Stonebridge Park!”

We meet midweek, and Kibo tells me he’s heading to a wrestling match in Dublin at the weekend. I ask him who he’s watching. “No, I’m wrestling,” he fires back: he’s up against Irish rapper Lil Skag, “to see who really is ready to hold the responsibility of being the champion of Ireland”. Kibo is 6ft 4in tall, possessing Irish heritage, a goatee, a mane of hair straight from a fantasy film, and a sackful of devastatingly rude bars: “I’ll take your mum Butlin’s / And I ain’t fucking bluffing / You’re not a bad boy, you’re an Egg McMuffin.” You’d back him to win a match on aura alone.

Add in references to anime, Pokémon, chicken shops and X-wing fighters, combine it with 16 producers making beats spanning garage, R&B, donk, grime and jungle, and you get a sense of Kwengletaria: Ragamyff’s scale. “I’m quite a maximalist guy, and a lot of the artists that I gravitate towards – Ghostface Killah, MF Doom, Yung Lean – it’s all about asking, how much can you stuff into one thing?” he says.

The all-you-can-eat impulse comes from growing up online – “I was a kid with a million tabs open, trying to speak with a level of eloquence” – and the Kwelengletarianism concept stems from when Kibo’s schoolmates began trading pirated Yu-Gi-Oh! cards. “They would slap even more glitter and shine on it, to make it look like it was the most valuable shit ever,” he says. “Like, I know this is fake, but this shit looks awesome. It’s the first thing I remember in my life where I was looking at something and knowing it was valuable.”

Kibo nods to his grime forebears on the album, sampling from Dizzee Rascal’s Boy in da Corner on closer Our War Game. “My absorption of grime was very retroactive,” he says. “Going back into Dizzee, Flirta D, Skepta, and D Double E … even though it was very local, it felt like discovering Three 6 Mafia, or old Memphis rap: like, this is awesome, but it’s not here.” Where those older acts felt remote to Kibo, Novelist, the Lewisham MC behind grime’s modern resurgence and Kwengletaria’s only guest, was “the first time I was able to tune into grime sets live and feel like I was present for this thing,” Kibo says. “It’s always felt like he was bringing grime back and pushing it forward.”

What’s impressive is how clear, satisfying and relentlessly funny Kibo’s path through the melee is. He shouts out Fiona Templeton, an academic at Brunel University (where he got a first in film, drama and media) for giving him a word for what he was doing: hyperdiction. “It was like someone showed me a brain scan,” he says. These collisions – of genres, references and words – create a new meta-language of smashed together non sequiturs in his work, such as “Courvoir-Sierra Leone”, or “Dimitar Burberrytov”. They’re also stamina-boosting power-ups. On Chancer, the album’s midpoint mellow grime flexer, Kibo’s criss-cross patterns unfold over three beat switches and five relentless verses.

On Bakerloo Dragon, Kibo says he gets the “charm from ma, and the swag from dad”. Eileen of Limerick fell swiftly in love with John, a drummer from Harrow, when he was over in Ireland for a holiday. They navigated a two-year long-distance relationship before she moved to England. “There was one phone box in her whole village, so it would be like, ‘You must be here at 7 o’clock.’ My dad used to work at the BT phone line so he was able to wrangle a few things.”

It made Kibo a true believer in romance. “It’s Kwengletarianism!” he says. “You’ve got to believe in something, you’ve got to believe there’s light at the end of the tunnel.” Kibo is a third generation member of Harrow’s Irish community, and there’s a distinctly Irish feeling to a project about belief, myths, good craic and finding the magic in ordinary objects.

Kwengletaria: Ragamyff is about celebrating where you’re from, but it’s also about feeling stuck in a place that, once the iridescent sheen has faded, is still grey and boring. Off the back of the album, and a medley of viral live clips, Kibo has his sights set beyond Harrow. “I feel like I finally got a grip of London. [The track] Red Starz is like, I’ve completed London, right? It’s almost like the post-credit scene is Ryanair: oh shit, there’s 200 other countries? Damn. There’s a crunch point there, between leaving home and returning. But if you find the magic and the pride in your base, you can always come back to that and recharge. Home is like your charging point.”

GeneralTab.title: Two ports denied request to land 120 migrants in RNLI boats
GeneralTab.text:
Requests to accept the landing of RNLI boats carrying 120 migrants intercepted off the Isle of Wight were refused by both Portsmouth harbour and Southampton Port.

When the migrants were landed on Sunday at Eastney, in Langstone Harbour, anti-migrant protesters blocked the road.

Associated British Ports (ABP), which operates Southampton, said it was not the closest port and it "did not have suitable reception facilities available".

The BBC understands the King's Harbour Master (KHM) Portsmouth also declined a coastguard request, but it would not comment directly on operational matters.

The protest followed a separate demonstration at the Port of Dover on the previous day.

The Langstone Harbour Master said the migrants were "recovered" onto two RNLI vessels in the vicinity of the Nab Tower.

They said they would have travelled at "quite a slow speed" to Langstone because the vessels were so overloaded.

An RNLI spokesperson said: "We are working with the relevant parties to understand the decision to deny access, and we are disappointed with the nature of the communication with our crews, who voluntarily give their time to save the lives of others at sea."

The narrow peninsula at Eastney has only one road leading in and out, which demonstrators used to block coaches carrying the migrants from leaving the area.

It led to a stand-off that lasted into the early hours of Monday.

Portsmouth City Council said it was a "completely unsuitable location to bring the boats ashore" and brought "needless disruption" to the area.

Langstone Harbour Master Billy Johnson said the coastguard was coordinating "a search and rescue operation" and there was "no reason not to accept" the landing of the vessels at Eastney.

"The problem was managing the public order aspect that was also taking place and the geography of the area made that very challenging for the police," he said.

"This is a new thing in the Solent and the degree to which it attracted public interest and the speed at which the public reaction was mobilised was unusual and surprising.

"The way the emergency services mobilised was really effective, with the police, Border Force, coastguard, the RNLI, ambulance and fire service working completely together - all of whom were hindered by the activities of protesters."

The leader of Portsmouth City Council, Steve Pitt, said: "The Home Office has some serious questions to answer about their lack of planning, inconsistent decision-making and ultimately, poor judgement."

In the House of Commons yesterday Dame Caroline Dinenage, Conservative MP for Portsmouth, referred to the boat containing 120 migrants in the Solent as an "extraordinary mega dinghy".

She said: "MPs across the Solent region were scrambling for reliable information with complete radio silence from the Home Office. As a result we weren't in a position to calm fear and tension."

Responding for the government, Home Office minister Sarah Jones said the department would "learn any lessons that we need to" following the weekend's protests.

Asked why Eastney had been chosen as the landing site, she said: "We are of course making sure we understand what exactly happened in that circumstance."

GeneralTab.title: Harry and Meghan 'surprised' by King's letter making clear they remain non-working royals
GeneralTab.text:
A spokesperson for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex says the couple were surprised to see a letter sent on behalf of King Charles clarifying that Prince Harry and Meghan remained non-working royals.

The spokesperson said the couple, who have recently moved back to the UK, "were a little surprised not to have been told about this in advance".

But royal sources say Prince Harry and Meghan were made aware of the letter, sent on Monday afternoon, before it was made public.

It is also understood a security committee, which includes Home Office representatives, is meeting this week to look at the level of taxpayer-funded security that should be given to the Sussexes who are now resident in the UK.

"The UK government's protective security system is rigorous and proportionate. It is our long-standing policy not to provide detailed information on those arrangements, as doing so could compromise their integrity and affect individuals' security," said a Home Office spokesperson.

They were believed to have had only had sight of the letter about an hour before it was shared with the media. By the time his team had made contact with Prince Harry it's understood the letter was almost published.

GeneralTab.title: Chris Rokos: UK's third-biggest taxpayer to leave for Greece
GeneralTab.text:
A hedge-fund billionaire and one of the UK's richest taxpayers has decided to leave the UK for Greece, the BBC understands.

Chris Rokos plans to open an office in Athens, according to reports. Greece has generous tax rules for wealthy foreigners earning overseas income.

Rokos was ranked third in The Sunday Times list of Britain's top taxpayers, having paid £330m last year, and in March said he would donate £190m to Cambridge University.

Rokos's representatives declined to comment. A government spokesperson said: "The UK remains an attractive destination for talent and investment".

"The chancellor has made wealth creation one of his top priorities," the spokesperson said, adding that the UK has "a competitive and stable tax system, deep capital markets, world-class universities and a highly skilled workforce".

It is not publicly known why Rokos has made the decision, which was first reported by Bloomberg, but Greece's tax-rules are seen as attractive to the ultra-wealthy.

They allow foreigners who meet certain criteria to pay a flat yearly tax of €100,000 (£86,000) on all overseas income.

Dan Neidle, the founder of the think tank Tax Policy Associates, told the BBC's Today programme that the £330m in tax revenue the UK could lose was "quite a lot of money".

"It is enough to fund 4,500 teachers... we have entire taxes that raise less than £330m."

"He will probably pay almost nothing in Greece, and we can't compete with that," he added.

Despite the potential loss, Neidle said there are "no easy answers and no good statistics" on the issue of ultra-wealthy taxpayers leaving the UK.

He said the Treasury has some estimates on the number of wealthy people leaving, but otherwise there are few facts about the true scale of the revenue loss.

"We have lots of anecdotes... what we don't really have is data," he said.

He said the government needed to "give certainty" to ultra-wealthy people living in the UK, arguing that lots of changes to the non-dom regime in a short space of time and reports of a possible wealth tax don't help.

"Stop rumours, stop tinkering," he said.

Rokos's decision comes ahead of UK Chancellor John Healey's first Budget on 28 October.

In an interview with the BBC on Monday, Healey did not rule out tax increases in the Budget, with a recent increase in government borrowing costs piling pressure on the public finances.

He refused to comment on any decisions about tax, promising only to "balance the books" and "control public spending".

In March, Cambridge University said the money from Rokos would be "the largest single donation made to a British university in modern times".

It will be used to create a school of government in Cambridge named after him with the aim of training leaders of the future. It is set to open this autumn.

Despite his generosity to Cambridge, Rokos is an Oxford graduate, having studied mathematics at Pembroke College.

He attended a state primary school before winning a scholarship to Eton College.

GeneralTab.title: 'Tirana teeth': Albania hopes to be the new Turkey for dental work
GeneralTab.text:
Anthony Hook is sitting in a dentist's chair, grinning toothily into a handheld mirror. He has been asked to pose for photos showing off his new smile – and he is only too happy to oblige.

The 58-year-old window cleaner from Bolton, in Greater Manchester, is the proud owner of a sparkling new set of "Tirana teeth".

That is not a brand name – at least, not yet. But it would be a fitting slogan as Albania moves decisively into the medical tourism business.

Tirana, its capital city, is the focus of operations. And once you spot the first tooth, you start seeing them everywhere. They seem to be all over the city centre.

Rest assured, these are not the physical remains from a night out that ended in a punch up. Rather, they are the kind of larger than life-size illuminated molar that – in these parts at least – advertise that a dental clinic is not too far away.

In Tirana's metropolitan area alone, there are almost four hundred dental clinics – and most of them are in the city centre. That's more than enough for a population of around 600,000 people.

So, it is not surprising that dozens of dentists are now targeting customers from further afield. They have set up websites and signage in English and Italian, as well as Albanian.

Dental implants in Albania are typically around €600 ($700; £516) per tooth, similar in price to what is charged in Turkey, which has long been the main overseas destination for people in western Europe who are seeking much cheaper dental work than they can get at home.

The same treatment in the UK, France or German can easily cost four times as much.

For Hook the appeal was irresistible. He made his first visit to Tirana to watch England's footballers play Albania last year – but then found himself intrigued by all the signs for dentists. That nudged him into doing something about his missing teeth.

He thought he's give Albania rather than Turkey, because he was concerned by media coverage of dental or hair transplant work in Turkey that had gone wrong.

In fact, even the UK Foreign Office warns that it is "aware of seven British nationals having died in Turkey in 2025 following medical procedures"., external It adds that "some British nationals have also experienced complications [after surgery in Turkey], and needed further treatment or surgery following their procedure."

Hook says he wouldn't go to Turkey "because I have heard so many bad things", adding that he investigated thoroughly before taking the plunge in Tirana.

"I went onto the internet and looked into it properly. It took me two days to research it because I'm not one for jumping into anything."

Several return trips later, Anthony now has a mouthful of impressive implants – and, unsurprisingly, he is all smiles. "I'd come here once a month for a holiday if I could," he chuckles.

Elite Dental is one of the biggest clinics in Tirana. It is fully licensed by the Albanian health authorities – and so are all of its 15 resident dentists.

The man who runs the place, Ardtur Dema, says he is "not in favour of damaging proper teeth for aesthetics". Instead he says the priority is "changing people's lives" through restoring their ability to chew, and indeed – to smile.

Dema believes that as long as Albania remains outside the EU, prices for treatment are likely to remain low. At the same time, low-cost airlines have greatly expanded their flight network to and from Tirana, meaning that he is as likely to see a patient from Turin as he is from Tirana.

But Dema is concerned that the explosion of tourism could lead to less scrupulous operators ruining the business for everyone. He is a member of the newly-established Albanian Medical Tourism Association – but many others are not, at least not yet.

Albania's Prime Minister, Edi Rama, tells the BBC that the government is playing catch-up after five years that have seen overall international arrivals to Albania more than double. Some sort of official seal of approval for medical tourism facilities is a possibility – but the government has yet to sort out the details.

"It's a new industry that is within the tourism industry umbrella that is showing a big potential and where there are very good people," says Rama.

He adds that the government wants to help all the reputable providers "survive", and to guard against any informal "bad competition".

Along with dental treatments, some visitors to Albania are starting to think "hairline" as well as "coastline".

Some transplant clinics are employing Turkish specialists – others are actually branches of businesses based in Turkey.

Vatanmed, in Tirana, is one of the latter. Sales specialist and health consultant Ayşe Mina Kasemi describes the business as a "global brand", with 15 clinics across a number of countries. That scale, she suggests, makes it "a safe place to trust" for the international patients arriving for treatment.

Besides that, Ayşe notes, Albania has its own appeal.

"When people decide to have a hair transplant operation here in Albania, they also want to have a holiday here, because Albania is a very beautiful place," she says, while adding a note of caution for hair transplant patients. "For the first two or three days, they have to be careful – they are not allowed to be exposed to the sun."

That is not a factor that concerns Anthony Hook. He happily sports a shaven head – and has no intention of following his dental treatment with a radical rug rethink. So enjoying Albania's beaches and scenery was very much part of the attraction of getting his teeth fixed here.

"There's a lot to do in Tirana… there's a lot to do along the coast there, it's absolutely stunning," he says. "I want to do it now before it gets too popular and it's ruined like everywhere else."

With his new teeth, enjoying Albania's cuisine will doubtless also be part of Anthony's programme. Apart from anything else, that smile is going to dazzle in the holiday snaps.

articles.title: Nottingham attacks victim's death potentially preventable, inquiry hears
articles.text:
The death of a student killed in the Nottingham attacks was "potentially preventable", a public inquiry has heard.

Barnaby Webber - along with Grace O'Malley-Kumar and Ian Coates - were killed by Valdo Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020, on 13 June 2023.

On Tuesday, ahead of closing statements to the Nottingham Inquiry, external - which is examining the killings - the inquiry was told a "more rapid administration of blood products" could have meant Barnaby's death was "potentially preventable".

The inquiry also heard documents found in a bin at Calocane's address contained a list of explosives, which was not disclosed by Nottinghamshire Police until June this year.

A panel of medical professionals assessed the emergency medical response on the day of the attacks to assess "survivability", the inquiry was told.

In their assessment, the panel noted the hard work of the emergency responders in their care to the victims.

The panel found if blood products had been administered to Barnaby earlier and more rapidly, it could have increased his chances of getting to hospital with enough of a heartbeat to undergo surgery.

However, multiple other rapid and particular steps would have had to have taken place for him to have survived.

The inquiry heard Barnaby had a less than 50% chance of surviving his injuries, characterised as "potentially preventable", while Grace and Ian's deaths were "not preventable".

The families of the victims sobbed as the assessments were read out by counsel to the inquiry Rachel Langdale KC. Grace's father, Dr Sanjoy Kumar, left the hearing room.

Langdale said Nottinghamshire Police found the documents in a bin at Calocane's former property in Burford Road in Nottingham.

He wrote bullet points on one page about explosives under the heading "thoughts", including TNT and nitrate fertiliser.

Langdale said: "This piece of paper listing thoughts about a number of explosives was not identified or taken into account at the time."

She added it had not been made available by police to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) or to psychiatric experts.

Calocane was evicted from the Burford Road address on 11 June 2023 and travelled to London, before returning via to Nottingham shortly before midnight on 12 June, a day before his killings, the inquiry heard.

The Nottingham Inquiry started hearing evidence in February, with more than 100 witnesses questioned over three months.

Witnesses included police staff and officers, mental healthcare practitioners, Calocane's former flatmates and family members, the bereaved families and the survivors of the attacks.

A number of revelations emerged in evidence about errors in Calocane's care, his previous interactions with police and failings both during and in the aftermath of the attacks.

Calocane - who also seriously injured three others - is currently serving an indefinite hospital order in a high-security facility after pleading guilty to three counts of manslaughter, on the grounds of diminished responsibility, and to three counts of attempted murder.

The inquiry is currently hearing updates in evidence since the end of oral evidence earlier this year.

In her closing remarks, Langdale reiterated the evidence of former parliamentary ombudsman Sir Rob Behrens.

She said: "Too often these cases are dependent upon bereaved families campaigning at a time when they are least prepared to do so, and it is an outstanding public service that they perform."

Langdale added: "Although Sir Rob was talking generally about bereaved families, his words could have been written as a description of the bereaved families and their legal team in this inquiry. Indeed, without their efforts there would not have been a public inquiry at all.

"The evidence we have obtained has revealed one failure after another.

"There is a suggestion in some submissions that further oral evidence should be called. We submit that there's no need for further oral evidence from any source.

"Barney, Grace and Ian should be alive. And the survivors - uninjured."

Final submissions to the chair, senior judge Deborah Taylor KC, will continue on Wednesday.

Taylor said it was "disappointing" that over the break, evidence had emerged which "ought to have been identified" and disclosed earlier.

She directed core participants to provide any corrections to errors or omissions by no later than 31 December.

Langdale said Nottinghamshire Police also recovered a holdall bag belonging to Calocane - who is being referred to in the inquiry as VC - from his address in the days after the attacks.

There were three notebooks in the bag, which included a note written by Calocane saying he was a god and "was a tree that guards the key between heaven and hell".

In his closing speech, Tim Moloney KC, who represents the bereaved families, said a note made by Calocane on one of the sheets of paper appeared to say "Manchester Arena".

Calocane searched online for large venues in Nottingham and bookmarks on his web browser for the Albert Hall Conference Centre in the city and the Theatre Royal and Royal Concert Hall, the inquiry heard.

Moloney said the notebooks also revealed "relevant information including what we say was a deep-seated misogyny".

The items were not prioritised because efforts were focused on finding a bag which the killer had with him on the evening of the attacks, the inquiry heard.

"There was a failure to investigate VC's historical behaviour and actions," Moloney said.

He added "no-one asked VC why he was searching for explosives and large venues because they couldn't", referencing the police's failure to share the information.

Langdale described the failure to disclose the notebooks an "oversight by Nottinghamshire Police".

The inquiry heard further violent assaults by Calocane on colleagues at warehouses in Nottinghamshire were also not disclosed to the inquiry team until after the public hearings took place.

This included an assault on a colleague in a warehouse in Eastwood in 2021 and another in Normanton in February 2023.

Footage of the February 2023 attack, described by Moloney as "sustained attack with punches thrown", was shown to the inquiry for the first time on Tuesday.

In his closing statement, Moloney focused on the timeline of contact between Calocane and public services.

"We say the timeline contains a litany of unnoticed red flags, missed opportunities and individual and systemic failures," he said.

"The bereaved families firmly believe that if opportunities had been taken to effectively deal with the behaviour of VC, if there had not been so many failures by so many people in institutions between 24 May 2020 and 13 June 2023, then their loved ones would still be here today.

"They have good reason to believe that, because VC's history of contact with public agencies is one of repeated individual and systemic failures in the face of the clear and growing risk that he presented."

Moloney said there were failures by authorities to follow policies and procedures and adequately consider harm with "every incident" involving Calocane between 2022 and 2023.

"Police were too quick to let things go in the teeth of really quite serious incidents, and clinicians were too quick to adopt a least restrictive practice which ignored the rights of his victims as we say ultimately and the rights of the public," he said.

"Together, these practices diverted VC away from the criminal justice system or forensic psychiatry and he should have been going down that pathway.

"Together, these practices failed VC and the people he affected who sit in this room."

Adam Straw KC, representing Calocane's family, highlighted a list of failings by Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust throughout the duration of its care for the triple killer.

He said: "Many of the problems brought to light by this case are founded on inadequate resources.

"It was clear from many of the witnesses at every level that resources for mental health services are far too low."

Among his suggestions, he said there should be a ring-fenced "increase for mental health service generally", national guidelines on minimum staffing levels for various relevant roles and more support for patients' families.

"Had VC received full and proper treatment and management of his admission in May 2020, there is reason to think that this tragedy would have been prevented.

"The same is true of many other schizophrenic-homicides up and down the country," Straw added.

articles.title: Monty Don to leave Gardeners' World after more than 20 years
articles.text:
Monty Don is to step down as the host of Gardeners' World after more than 20 years, the BBC has announced.

The 71-year-old, who is the programme's longest-serving head gardener, will leave at the end of the current series.

In a statement, Don said working on the show had been a "deeply rewarding experience," but added: "Now is the right time for a change."

The BBC said Don had "inspired and guided millions of viewers with his warmth, wisdom and passion for gardening" since joining the programme in 2003.

Don began presenting the programme at Berryfields, a rented garden in Stratford-upon-Avon, before it moved in 2011 to his own garden, Longmeadow in Herefordshire.

"Throughout that time - and around 700 programmes - I have had the privilege of sharing my own abiding passion for gardens and gardening with an equally passionate, and often equally knowledgeable audience," he said.

"That connection with millions, not just in Britain but across the world, who share a love of gardens, plants and the natural world is something I have always treasured and which I increasingly believe to be at the heart of a life well lived."

Don added he had "always relished the craft of programme making" and paid tribute to the "superlative BBC team" he worked with over the years.

"I look forward to continuing to work with and for the BBC on other projects, as well as following new avenues," he concluded. "And of course, I will still be gardening, dog by side, here at Longmeadow."

articles.title: Prince George begins first day at Eton College
articles.text:
Prince George arrived on a rainy morning for his first day at Eton College, accompanied by his father and mother, the Prince and Princess of Wales.

Prince William and Catherine carried umbrellas as they brought George, wearing a jacket and tie, to be welcomed by the head teacher, Simon Henderson, and provost Sir Nicholas Coleridge.

"Welcome, good luck and enjoy," said the head teacher, shaking hands with Prince George.

They made small talk about the bad weather before the new pupil, parents and staff disappeared inside the historic school, where 13-year-old George will be a boarder.

George, who had travelled the short journey from his home at Forest Lodge in Windsor, was seen with his parents arriving at Eton's school yard, overlooked by the school's Tudor landmark of Lupton's Tower.

He was later photographed wearing the school's uniform, with black tailcoat, waistcoat and a stiff white collar.

The future king follows in the footsteps of his father in attending the elite private school, which has taught 20 British prime ministers and where fees are around £65,000 a year.

articles.title: England up in reading, maths and science rankings as Scotland and Wales dip
articles.text:
English pupils have pulled ahead of the rest of the UK in international reading, maths and science tests, new data suggests, with Scotland and Wales falling further behind.

The 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) saw reading and maths scores slump in each UK nation except England, while all four saw an uptick in science, with that rise again most notable in England.

The latest Pisa report, which is published every three years, also warned of a worldwide decline in teenagers' reading skills.

Teenagers were losing the skills that "matter most in the age of AI", such as being able to critically evaluate information from different sources, it said.

The share of "hasty readers", who rush through texts to give quick, incorrect answers, has almost doubled between 2018 and 2025. The report warned the fall was greatest in those from "relatively well off" families.

Run by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), the Pisa tests assess teenagers on their ability to solve problems, think critically and communicate, before asking them a wider range of questions about their education in a questionnaire.

Although the UK performed well overall, the rankings varied significantly again, with results showing England, where the curriculum is significantly different, pulling consistently ahead of Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.

England's schools minister, Georgia Gould, said the government wanted to "build on" the positive results and "go further so all young people leave school with strong literacy and numeracy".

The 2025 Pisa tests were taken by a sample of 760,000 15-year-olds in 91 countries. In the UK, where education differs between the home nations, 15,566 students took the tests in 515 schools.

In England, where it was recently announced that technical subjects would soon be available to students from age 14, Gould held up high-performing Estonia as an example of where "academic excellence can go hand in hand with high-quality vocational routes".

"Our reforms will build on England's strong academic foundations so future generations not only perform well, but feel connected to school and excited about where their education can take them," she added.

But Laura Trott, England's shadow education secretary, said the country's successes were down to previous reforms, and accused the new government of trying to "sabotage" them.

While Wales lags behind the rest of the UK overall, on science it is ahead of other European countries such as France, Spain and the Netherlands.

As the tests last year were taken by 15-year-olds, the results there largely reflect learning under an old curriculum, which has recently been changed.

Anna Brychan, Wales' minister for education and Welsh language, said plans were in place to support schools, adding that the results "highlight our need to improve standards of reading and maths, as a priority".

Scotland's education secretary, Mairi McAllan, said the results showed "real strengths in Scottish education, as well as areas we're already working to improve".

But Scottish Labour said results had "flatlined since 2022's historically poor results", while the Scottish Liberal Democrats said the education system under the SNP had "tumbled down the rankings, lagging behind England on every measure of performance".

Northern Ireland's education minister, Paul Givan, said pupils there had performed well by international standards, but that - like other countries - its education system was facing "significant challenges", adding that "there is much more work to do".

Overall, the Pisa tests provide the biggest global snapshot of education systems and an independent view of how teenagers are performing compared with their peers in other countries, so it is a relative measure.

articles.title: Borrowers expecting mortgage rates to drop have hopes dashed
articles.text:
Nearly all the major mortgage lenders in the UK have announced increases in the cost of home loans in recent days.

Analysts are uncertain over whether there are more to come, but are urging people who need to find a new deal to act now.

Someone whose five-year deal is coming to an end faces paying more than £5,000 more a year on their next deal under a typical rate, if they borrow the same amount of money.

Many lenders allow people to lock in a new deal six months before their current one comes to an end, with an opportunity to switch if the costs come down before it kicks in.

"Borrowers expecting mortgage rates to drop in the coming weeks have had their hopes dashed," said Rachel Springall, from financial information service Moneyfacts.

"It is still essential borrowers do not delay seeking advice to navigate the mortgage maze."

For borrowers, the interest rate on a fixed mortgage does not change until it expires, usually after two or five years, and a new one is chosen to replace it. The vast majority of homeowners and buyers have this kind of mortgage.

Since the Iran war began, global economic uncertainty has pushed up the cost of deals.

Speaking to MPs on the Treasury Committee, Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said UK borrowers had seen the biggest rise in mortgage rates, apart from Japan, since the conflict started than in other countries in the G7 group of major economic powers.

Someone on a typical two-year deal, and borrowing £250,000 is likely to pay £120 more a month in mortgage repayments than they would have had they secured the deal at the start of March when the US-Israeli strikes began, according to Moneyfacts.

More recently, UK government borrowing costs have been rising, which has a knock-on impact on mortgage rates.

That pressure has been maintained in the latest sale of debt by the UK on Tuesday. A 30-year bond issued by the UK was sold with a yield - or interest rate - of 5.82%, the highest since 1998.

The situation has resulted in several major lenders raising their rates in the last few days.

"The difficult bit is knowing whether this is the end or just the first round of increases," said David Hollingworth, from broker L&C.

articles.title: Liam Gallagher's tambourine grin and Charli XCX says bye to Brat - Music Photography Awards 2026 shortlist
articles.text:
Striking images of Oasis's reunion tour and Charli XCX bringing Brat to Glastonbury Festival are among the nominees at this year's Abbey Road Music Photography Awards.

The awards, which this year considered works by more than 24,500 submissions from 42 different countries, released a shortlist of 40 finalists across eight categories on Tuesday.

The likes of Kendrick Lamar, Fontaines DC, Tame Impala and Sombr also feature in the shots, while other images of stars including FKA Twigs have been selected - out of competition - for judges' awards.

All of the finalist photographs will go on display in the LED tunnel at entertainment complex Outernet London from 8 to 14 September.

These will include the five pieces picked out for consideration in the fan-voted music moment of the year award.

Voting is available online via the official website, external, and in person at the exhibition.

The winners will be announced at a ceremony at the London studios - made famous by the 1969 Beatles album of the same name - on 24 September.

Head judge, British photographer and director Rankin, said 2026 "feels like the strongest year yet" for the awards, which began five years ago.

"The quality of the work entered was genuinely exceptional - not just technically brilliant, but full of energy, emotion and a real point of view."

He added: "Music photography is in a really exciting place right now, and these awards are a brilliant snapshot of that."

This year's guest category celebrates 50 years of punk.

It was previously announced that photographers Roberta Bayley and Masayoshi Sukita will both receive special recognition on the night.

The judging panel includes artists from around the worlds of music and photography, including Chic guitarist and producer Nile Rogers and Brit Award-winning singer Raye.

articles.title: In West Bank, date farmers weigh impact of UK sanctions on Israeli settlers
articles.text:
Juicy brown and ripening yellow dates dangle down from the branches of each palm tree at Israeli settler farms in the Jordan Valley, in the occupied West Bank.

This year, as Israeli growers get ready for a good harvest, they are also preparing for the impact of new Western sanctions against settlements, which are illegal under international law.

The UK government has announced an import ban on settlement goods and said it planned to take action against companies and individuals who provide services for settlement expansion, as part of what it calls a "comprehensive reset" of policy towards Israel following similar moves by several other European countries.

Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden have also confirmed their intention to introduce national restrictions, or support European restrictions, on trade in goods with settlements.

Palestinians strongly back such a move, but Israel's foreign minister called it "hostile" and announced a series of counter measures, including the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem.

Israeli date farmer Avigdor Arbel, from the settlement of Mesua, calls such boycotts "really disgusting".

Arbel sells his produce mostly to Europe but also to the US and now, India. However, he says the sector is ready for any new UK ban on settler goods.

"As soon as we have a situation of pressure and boycotts, we always break out and look for other markets," he tells me. "So, I believe that if we get to a situation in which there's no place to sell my fruits in Europe, we'll find other markets."

West Bank settlements have expanded rapidly under the current Israeli government, whose ministers say they want "to bury the idea" of an independent Palestinian state - part of the long-standing international formula for peace in the region known as the two-state solution.

At the same time, settler violence against Palestinians has surged to what the UN says is "an all-time high".

With new settler outposts - which are also illegal under Israeli law - now dotting the barren hilltops of the Jordan Valley, there have been repeated attacks on local Palestinians, particularly Bedouin and herding communities.

In January, the last of some 600 villagers fled their homes in Ras Ein al-Ouja after intense harassment by hardline settlers, often backed by Israeli security forces. It was the largest single displacement of a Palestinian community in the past three years.

Further north, in March, Israeli settlers brutally beat and sexually assaulted a Palestinian shepherd during a night raid on Khirbet Humsa.

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Parliament on Tuesday that a set of facts on the ground had been created "to make the two-state solution unviable," while "settler terrorism is rampant".

Quoting a former Israeli minister of health and retired brigadier general, Ephraim Sneh, he said the UK government "agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank perpetrated by settler terrorists", to which the Israeli government had "turned a blind eye" or actually supported.

In a significant change of UK policy, he said the government now agreed with the 2024 International Court of Justice advisory opinion that Israel's continued occupation "is unlawful".

As a consequence, Miliband said this should be reflected "in the economic relationships we choose to have with the occupied territories".

"I do not believe that the British people want us supporting the occupation by accepting products from settlements in our shops and supermarkets."

Medjool dates are the main export crop from both Israeli settler farms and Palestinian farms in the Jordan Valley.

"These are rubbish," says Palestinian farmer Abdul Halim Abu Omar, dramatically reaching up and throwing away a handful of shrivelled, yellow dates from a tree in the grove where he works in al-Ouja, north of Jericho.

Around half of the date palms here have no fruit at all. "It's because we lack water," Abu Omar says. His is an extreme case: this year, the trees he cares for have received less than a third of the water they need to thrive.

Access to water has long been a pressing issue in the West Bank.

Interim peace agreements from the 1990s have left a water disparity between Israelis and Palestinians, and Israeli authorities typically prioritise water for settlers over Palestinians' needs.

Recently, in rural areas of the Jordan Valley, almost all of which is under Israeli security and civilian control, extremist settlers have also taken over several freshwater springs.

The Israeli Civil Administration told the BBC that it keeps "continuous contact" with the Palestinian Water Authority and assists in carrying out repairs to water infrastructure.

This harvest time, Abu Omar has few dates that are fit to show local Palestinian exporter Momen Sinokrot. His firm, Palestine Gardens, works with 55 date growers in the Jordan Valley to sell to several European countries, including the UK.

Sinokrot believes that if more states ban settlement trade this could curb settlement growth.

"Settlers are very active in the Jordan Valley... and they are not obeying any laws or rules or anything even from the Israeli army itself," he says.

"They are going to the fields of the growers, they are stealing from them, and they are controlling more and more land."

There have been questions raised about how a ban on settlement goods would be enforced.

A recent report by the legal advocacy group Global Echo found that some settlement fruits and vegetables sold in Europe were inaccurately identified as coming from Israel - or mingled with produce from inside Israel's internationally-recognised borders.

However, the report's author, Jessica Stober, suggests that a UK ban on settler goods would greatly increase the financial costs associated with any such fraudulent practices. Instead of a seller being fined for misrepresenting their goods, the shipment would be returned.

"A ban is more self-enforcing because you have involved the private sector and it becomes commercially unviable for them to deal in settlement goods," Stober says.

"I would also say that a whole new set of measures become available to the UK government under a sanctions regime, under a ban, including civil and criminal penalties that make compliance much more likely."

Israel's Foreign Minister, Gideon Saar, responded quickly to the UK's announcement, branding the move "morally distorted" and constituting a "blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and in its electoral process", referring to Israel's general election in late October.

He announced "a series of Israeli countermeasures", including the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem and the removal of British representatives from the US-led International Gaza Support Center (IGSC) in Kiryat Gat, which is in charge of co-ordinating the shaky ceasefire in the Gaza Strip.

"The message to every government that harms us is clear: whoever acts against Israel, Israel will act against them, and they will lose their influence and relevance in the region," Saar warned.

Last month, Israel expelled two Dutch diplomats from the IGSC, after the Netherlands banned trade from settlements.

Other European countries that have already imposed a ban on settlement goods or trade restrictions - arguing it is a legal obligation - include Ireland, Spain and Belgium.

Now, the new action by the UK looks set to put a new, heavy strain on its relations with Israel.

articles.title: Maryam Moshiri: BBC News presenter reveals she has blood cancer
articles.text:
BBC News presenter Maryam Moshiri has revealed she is living with blood cancer.

Moshiri, who joined the BBC in 2003 and is one of the news channel's best-known anchors, told the BBC she wanted to share her diagnosis to raise awareness about the disease.

"It's been two years since my diagnosis and I've felt that I've started to understand the disease a lot better and the way it affects my life. I've got a handle on it to a degree now, so I felt it was really important to raise awareness," the 49-year-old said.

"I'm going to have to spend the rest of my life being treated for this," she added.

Moshiri was diagnosed in November 2024 with polycythaemia vera (PV) - a rare, treatable blood cancer. Although it cannot be cured, it can be managed effectively.

In PV, your body makes too many red blood cells, which makes the blood thicker than normal.

It leads to a higher risk of developing blood clots, which can cause a stroke, heart attack or deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

Symptoms can include headaches, confusion, dizziness and blurred vision.

"I was told by my consultant that I have this incurable blood cancer," she said.

"Mostly I had no symptoms and that's one of the problems with this disease.

"The only reason mine was caught was because my GP was so fastidious in the way she did my routine blood tests and immediately sent them for further diagnosis."

As part of her initial treatment, the BBC News chief presenter underwent several "debilitating" hour-long sessions of venesections.

Venesection is a procedure where a needle is put into a vein in the arm to slowly draw the blood out.

This blood letting can be an effective way to reduce the thickness of the blood.

"In about a space of five months, I had venesection seven or eight times. So you can imagine my iron levels hit the floor and I felt even more exhausted," she said.

"After a while I started feeling extremely unwell and tired. I started losing my hair, I got itchy all over my body, but the main symptom was fatigue."

Later, The World Today presenter was able to get on an immunotherapy treatment called interferon through the NHS, and after some tweaks, she says she is in a better place.

"I've only needed one venosection in about 15 months, so that's been really good. The last couple of months have been better than the last two years," she said.

"I think it's really important people understand that this blood cancer is incurable but it's manageable with the right treatment and you can lead a relatively healthy life.

"It's just a question of finding the right treatment and making sure it works for you."

She admits she is "not the person I was two years ago" but says she feels "much better".

The mother-of-three said she has had to adjust to life with her condition, sometimes not being able to attend family occasions or play with her children because she is exhausted.

"It's the kind of fatigue that is not like I'm just tired and I didn't get a good night's sleep, you feel like someone has removed your battery completely, and however much sleep you get makes no difference," she explains.

"Even though I feel the best I have in two years, I don't know how I'm going to be in six months, one year, two years.

"People with PV have a higher chance of stroke, heart attack or DVT, so it's something I always have to be aware of and make sure I mitigate."

Despite the fatigue, Moshiri has continued to travel across the world covering the biggest stories over the last two years for the BBC, anchoring from Qatar at the start of the US-Israel war with Iran, covering the selection of the new Pope from the Vatican and travelling to Greenland for Vice-President JD Vance's visit.

She credits her "supportive and helpful" husband Jonathan, management at the BBC and her children Iris, 13, Vivienne, 11 and Caspian, 9.

"It took me a long time to be able to tell them about this illness, because I don't want to worry them, but they have been so understanding. When I say things like 'mummy is too tired to play with you', they get it and they don't push it," she said.

Helen Rowntree, chief executive of Blood Cancer UK, said: "We're so grateful to Maryam for bravely sharing her story. When public figures speak openly about their diagnosis, it cuts through the silence that so often surrounds blood cancer – the UK's fifth most common cancer and third biggest cancer killer."

Rowntree said blood cancer can feel like a "silent" cancer as patients can present with vague, hard to spot symptoms, and highlighted that many with the disease manage their illness, treatment and side-effects alongside work and family life.

"We urgently need continued public and government support to fund the next generation of kinder, more effective treatments with fewer side-effects – so that more people with blood cancer can live well, spend less time dealing with the impact of treatment and be there for the moments that matter," she added.

"There is a lot of research going into blood cancer and scientific advancement to look forward to. Hopefully they'll be some sort of advancement that will help even more than these medications I've been given," Moshiri added.

articles.title: Ukrainian TV channel building hit by Russian drone as five killed in Kyiv
articles.text:
A Russian drone has struck a Ukrainian TV channel headquarters in Kyiv, injuring at least five people as journalists were broadcasting live, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

Zelensky said the daytime attack was a "new page in Russian degradation", while photos shared by the president show a partially collapsed building.

At least five people have been killed in overnight and daytime Russian strikes on Kyiv, while a separate attack on a passenger train in southern Ukraine killed a female employee, officials have said.

Both countries had earlier agreed to halt strikes on each other's capitals for three days while US Donald Trump's top envoys visited Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend.

Referring to Tuesday's Russian drone attack on the Ukrainian TV channel We Are Ukraine, Zelensky said: "Today, Russia carried out a strike on the media, journalists.

"Russia must be stopped, and this is possible only through joint efforts," he added in a renewed plea to Ukraine's allies in Europe, the US and around the world.

Earlier on Tuesday, air raid alerts warned civilians to seek shelter as Russian forces carried out missile and drone strikes on Kyiv, the local authorities said.

A series of explosions across Ukraine's capital overnight killed three people and injured another 25, the state emergencies service DSNS said.

Residential buildings were hit, including a five-storey house in the Solomianskyi district, while vehicles caught fire in the Podilskyi district.

People sought shelter inside a metro station in Kyiv during the overnight attack, something that is routine for residents protecting themselves during the ongoing war.

By Tuesday afternoon, the death toll had reached five people.

According to a BBC Verify analysis, Kyiv is suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's full-scale invasion.

In Russia, buildings were struck in the city of Saratov during a Ukrainian drone attack, its regional governor Roman Busargin said early on Tuesday.

The talks with Trump's top envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow and Kyiv ended without any major breakthroughs.

Zelensky said he expected the war to continue into the winter, following the envoys' first visit to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

In Moscow, President Vladimir Putin's senior adviser Yuriy Ushakov said the US envoys were informed about "the significant advances made by the Russian armed forces" on the battlefield and stressed that the Kremlin's "set objectives would be achieved".

Putin has so far showed no sign of backing down from his maximalist demands, which included more territorial concessions from Ukraine.

Meanwhile, Witkoff said that "substantive progress was made", without giving any further details.

Zelensky told reporters they had agreed that officials from Ukraine, Europe and America would meet in the near future to continue discussions. He also called for a trilateral meeting with Russia and the US.

articles.title: Chris Rokos: UK's third-biggest taxpayer to leave for Greece
articles.text:
A hedge-fund billionaire and one of the UK's richest taxpayers has decided to leave the UK for Greece, the BBC understands.

Chris Rokos plans to open an office in Athens, according to reports. Greece has generous tax rules for wealthy foreigners earning overseas income.

Rokos was ranked third in The Sunday Times list of Britain's top taxpayers, having paid £330m last year, and in March said he would donate £190m to Cambridge University.

Rokos's representatives declined to comment. A government spokesperson said: "The UK remains an attractive destination for talent and investment".

"The chancellor has made wealth creation one of his top priorities," the spokesperson said, adding that the UK has "a competitive and stable tax system, deep capital markets, world-class universities and a highly skilled workforce".

It is not publicly known why Rokos has made the decision, which was first reported by Bloomberg, but Greece's tax-rules are seen as attractive to the ultra-wealthy.

They allow foreigners who meet certain criteria to pay a flat yearly tax of €100,000 (£86,000) on all overseas income.

Dan Neidle, the founder of the think tank Tax Policy Associates, told the BBC's Today programme that the £330m in tax revenue the UK could lose was "quite a lot of money".

"It is enough to fund 4,500 teachers... we have entire taxes that raise less than £330m."

"He will probably pay almost nothing in Greece, and we can't compete with that," he added.

Despite the potential loss, Neidle said there are "no easy answers and no good statistics" on the issue of ultra-wealthy taxpayers leaving the UK.

He said the Treasury has some estimates on the number of wealthy people leaving, but otherwise there are few facts about the true scale of the revenue loss.

"We have lots of anecdotes... what we don't really have is data," he said.

He said the government needed to "give certainty" to ultra-wealthy people living in the UK, arguing that lots of changes to the non-dom regime in a short space of time and reports of a possible wealth tax don't help.

"Stop rumours, stop tinkering," he said.

Rokos's decision comes ahead of UK Chancellor John Healey's first Budget on 28 October.

In an interview with the BBC on Monday, Healey did not rule out tax increases in the Budget, with a recent increase in government borrowing costs piling pressure on the public finances.

He refused to comment on any decisions about tax, promising only to "balance the books" and "control public spending".

In March, Cambridge University said the money from Rokos would be "the largest single donation made to a British university in modern times".

It will be used to create a school of government in Cambridge named after him with the aim of training leaders of the future. It is set to open this autumn.

Despite his generosity to Cambridge, Rokos is an Oxford graduate, having studied mathematics at Pembroke College.

He attended a state primary school before winning a scholarship to Eton College.
